 Enjoy unlimited access to all of our incredible journalism, in print and digital. Subscribe Now News United Methodist Bishop Names New Highland Park Pastor After Separation Vote 
 Days after members voted to leave the United Methodist Church, Bishop Ruben Saenz Jr. appointed Rev. Andy Lewis to lead those who want to remain. By Bethany Erickson | October 29, 2026 | 12:09 pm Share Copy Link Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Email Comment Add D Magazine on Google Add D Magazine as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google. Anita Moti Advertisement Live Poll 
 Live Poll 
 Just days after Highland Park United Methodist Church members voted to leave the denomination over a dispute regarding the church’s bylaws, it has a new minister.
 In an announcement released today, Bishop Ruben Saenz Jr., who is the head of both the Horizon Texas Conference and the United Methodist Council of Bishops, said that he has appointed Rev. Andy Lewis as senior pastor of the church. Saenz also said he has “reappointed…from all positions” Rev. Matt Tuggle, the Highland Park UMC senior minister who has become the face of the effort to leave the denomination, along with former senior minister Paul Rasmussen. The move was effective October 29. Highland Park UMC has not yet responded to a request for comment.
 After two days of voting, 4,775 members cast votes, with more than 90 percent voting to leave the denomination , identifying itself as Highland Park Methodist Church. The resolution preceding the vote, first recites the history of the dispute. It then outlines the steps it will take to potentially remove itself from the United Methodist Church in a church-wide vote “as defined in the Church’s Bylaws,” adding that “the Church Council has reached the conclusion that the time is right to recommend that the Church sever all affiliation with the UMC while preserving the historic ministry and mission of the Church and continuing the Church’s faithful adherence to Wesleyan Methodist theological tradition.”
 The church, which has roughly 15,000 members, has been a United Methodist (or its predecessors) congregation for more than a century. In 2022, Highland Park UMC changed its bylaws, removing references to the denomination and its governing principles known as the Book of Discipline. On August 10, the denomination’s Horizon Texas Conference filed suit against the church, asking the court to rule that Highland Park UMC should either amend its new bylaws to align with the Book of Discipline or revert to the version the church passed in 1998. A later amended suit outlined attempts by Horizon Texas Conference Bishop Ruben Saenz Jr. to convince church leadership to change the bylaws before filing suit. Later, the conference accused the church of breach of contract. It asks for the court to issue an injunction. In a statement to the Dallas Morning News , the conference said that the United Methodist Church’s clergy and lay people are in a shared covenant “with responsibilities to one another beyond any single congregation … Honoring this covenant begins with upholding the vows we have made as United Methodists and restoring Highland Park’s governing documents to reflect those shared commitments.” 
 The church says it would like to complete its work in separating from the denomination by the end of the year. 
 Saenz’s announcement comes with some caveats. For one, members of the Highland Park United Methodist Church who plan to worship with Lewis will be doing so at University Park United Methodist Church at 10 a.m. on Sunday. This is likely because, thanks to the vote and the ongoing litigation, the thorny issue of who controls the church property is probably also headed to court. The United Methodist denomination operates under a legal and doctrinal provision that allows churches great latitude in how they maintain and improve their properties, but property is held in a trust for the benefit of the entire denomination, which is why control of the Highland Park property is such a consequential part of the dispute. The decision to temporarily worship up the street “reflects a desire to respect everyone involved and avoid unnecessary conflict as the Conference continues to address questions surrounding Highland Park UMC’s governance and property.”
 The conference also says that Highland Park UMC can’t actually vote to leave the denomination as easily as other churches have. The mechanism for allowing that, called disaffiliation, was only open for a a brief time as the denomination navigated internecine disputes over doctrine related to same-sex marriage and LGBTQ clergy. That period expired in 2023. While Highland Park UMC did change its bylaws during that time period, it did not follow the steps outlined to fully disaffiliate from the denomination. Highland Park UMC leadership acknowledged this early on, explaining that the move to change the bylaws was to “protect” the church, not leave it.
 “Many of you voted no. Many of you spoke up, met with your pastors and told your church’s leaders, respectfully and clearly, that you disagreed with the direction they were taking. That took courage,” Saenz wrote. “I know this has been painful. The church you love is more than a building or a place you attend on Sunday mornings. It is where you have worshiped, raised your children, celebrated life’s joys and found comfort in times of sorrow. The relationships you have built and the faith you have shared there are deeply personal, making the uncertainty about your church’s future especially painful.” (You can read the full letter here .)
 The move to provide a way to worship together was important for those who opposed the move. “My immediate concern is for you and your continued life together as a worshiping community,” he wrote. “I do not want faithful United Methodists of Highland Park to go a single Sunday without a place to gather, worship God and share in the fellowship that has sustained you for generations.”
 Lewis is a longtime assistant to the bishop, first at the North Texas Conference and now in the Horizon Texas Conference. Saenz says he assisted in forming the latter, which combined three conferences after the disaffiliation period. He also was a founding pastor of a new church in McKinney that cared for families displaced by Hurricane Katrina, and later served as senior pastor of Holy Covenant UMC in Carrollton and First United Methodist Church Lewisville. He will lead worship at a church in flux, helping those who did not wish to leave to remain connected with the denomination.
 “In the midst of a hard season, I look forward to providing pastoral care that will help the congregation find healing and leadership that will restore trust and hope,” Lewis said in a statement. His first sermon will take place at 10 a.m. Sunday.
